sentences.h1: More than half of first pull requests hear nothing for two weeks. About 1 in {one_in_14} of those still gets merged.
sentences.lede: Porchlamp followed {first} first pull requests, each from someone who hadn't sent that project a pull request in about the previous six months or longer. About 1 in {one_in_0} gets merged. Silence lowers those odds fast at first and more slowly after: {merged_7} after a week, {merged_14} after two weeks, {merged_30} after a month, {merged_60} after two months.

sentences.wait_heading: Two weeks of silence cuts the odds by more than half
sentences.wait_text: Each point counts pull requests at least four months old that had no answer by that day, and how many of them were merged in the end. After two months of silence the two lines nearly meet, at {merged_60} and {returning_merged_60}.
sentences.late_text: A late answer is still possible. Of first pull requests silent at two weeks, {later_30} hear something by day 30, {later_60} by day 60 and {later_90} by day 90.
sentences.wait_note: Share merged by the end of the data, at least four months after opening, by days with no answer. {first_settled} first pull requests are old enough to count. An answer means a reply or review from the project's people, a merge, or a close by them.
sentences.ask_heading: Authors who asked got about {ask_gap} points more answers. Other comments got none.
sentences.ask_text: Of first pull requests silent at two weeks, {ask_answered} got an answer in the next 30 days if the author had asked in the past week, with words like "friendly ping" or "could you take a look". With no comment at all it was {ask_answered_none}. Part of that gap comes from which projects get asked. Inside one project, about {ask_gap} points remain. A comment that didn't ask shows nothing.
sentences.ask_note: First pull requests silent at two weeks, {ask_n} with a recent ask in {ask_projects} projects. Lines show the 95% range. Across all outside pull requests the same comparison gives {all_ask_gap} points ({all_ask_low} to {all_ask_high}) for asking, from {all_ask_n} pull requests in {all_ask_projects} projects, and {all_other_gap} points ({all_other_low} to {all_other_high}) for a comment that didn't ask.
sentences.merges_text: Merges follow: {ask_merged} merged against {ask_merged_none}, or {ask_merged_gap} points inside one project ({ask_merged_low} to {ask_merged_high}). An ask in the first week shows less: {week_one_gap} points ({week_one_low} to {week_one_high}), measured at one week.
sentences.first_heading: The first pull request waits longest
sentences.first_text: Within a day, {answered_1d} of first pull requests have an answer, against {returning_answered_1d} for people the project has seen before. After two weeks the gap is still there: {answered_14d} against {returning_answered_14d}.
sentences.first_note: Share answered by each point in time, log scale, allowing for pull requests too young to tell or closed by their author. {first} first and {returning} returning pull requests.
sentences.week_text: Inside the same project, weekday pull requests beat weekend ones in {weekday_better} of {weekday_projects} projects, by a median of {weekday_gap} points.
sentences.week_note: All outside pull requests, days in UTC. The inside-a-project figure uses projects with at least 30 weekday and 10 weekend pull requests. Weekend senders may differ from weekday ones, which that comparison only partly removes.
sentences.who_heading: In most projects, one person is doing the answering
sentences.who_text: In {over_half} of {who_projects} projects, one person gave more than half of the first answers to outsiders. The median project has {median_people} people answering at all. Fame barely changes it: among {large_projects} projects with {large_stars} stars or more, it's {large_over_half}, with a median of {large_people} people.
sentences.who_note: Projects by the busiest person's share of first answers, for projects with at least 20 first answers we could attribute to a person. Bots are left out. In {top_bin} projects, one person gave at least 90%.
sentences.fast_heading: {count_title} projects that answer first-timers quickly and merge their work
sentences.fast_text: Picked by hand from the {listed_projects} projects with at least 25 first pull requests old enough to judge, so this isn't a ranking. All {count_word} answered at least {min_within_a_day} of them within a day and merged at least {min_merged}. Most have under 60 first pull requests, so read them as examples. Each link opens the project's Porchlamp page.
method: Data. Porchlamp's {snapshot_id} snapshot holds {outside_prs} outside pull requests opened from {window_start} to {window_end}, across {projects} projects with a record. These results read {read} of them, those with recorded replies after the rules below. An earlier post's 212,390 came from a smaller read of the same projects, before the collection was widened.
Left out. Bots, project members, drafts never marked ready, and accounts under {min_account_days} days old. In very busy projects, replies are read from the snapshot's even random sample.

First pull request. The author has no earlier pull request to that project in its 365-day record, which looks back about six months or more from any pull request here. Only projects whose record isn't cut off at its cap of about 500 can tell, so the busiest projects are missing. The split covers {known} of the {read} pull requests read, {known_share}.

Which results use what. The waiting curve, the answered-by curve and the listed projects use first pull requests only. So do the asking figures unless a line says all outside pull requests. The weekday and who-answers results use all outside pull requests.
An answer. The earliest reply or review from the project's people, a merge, or a close by them. Replies from bots don't count, and the clock starts when a draft is marked ready.

Asking. A comment from the author after the first hour, matched against a word list: ping, bump, gentle nudge, could you review, take a look, any update and similar. A hand check of 50 matches found 47 real asks. Tool commands and CLA signatures don't count. The baseline is no comment at all. The inside-one-project gap compares the groups project by project, weighted by how many each has (Mantel-Haenszel), and the 95% range comes from resampling projects. We tightened the word list after a first look at the data, so this is a result to test again on the next snapshot.

Waiting curve. Pull requests at least four months old. One an author closed unanswered drops out from that day. The {silent_14} near the top uses all {first} and treats an author closing their own pull request as leaving the count, so it doesn't divide out from the curve's table.
not_covered: Why a project didn't answer. Silence may mean a closed list, a mailing-list workflow, or a pull request nobody wanted.
Not seen. Merges after the record's date, and any pull request's quality or size.
Cause. All of this describes what happened, including the asking and weekday comparisons. Authors who ask may also care more, or have a better pull request.
Six months is one season. Volume and answer rates may move with the time of year.
sentences.black_holes_differ: Porchlamp's black-holes report says more than 1 in {black_hole_one_in} projects leave most outsiders with nothing for two weeks. This report's 1 in {one_in_14} counts pull requests merged after that silence. They're different numbers.
sentences.cite: Porchlamp. First pull requests: who answers and how long it takes. Snapshot {snapshot_id}, data from {window_start} to {window_end}. {page_url}
sentences.description: Porchlamp followed {first} first pull requests. {silent_14} heard nothing for two weeks, about 1 in {one_in_14} of those still got merged, and asking went with more answers.
sentences.title: More than half of first pull requests hear nothing for two weeks
